text: Patriarchy, patriarchy, patriarchy. If you listen to some modern feminists, it can sound like men today live in paradise and women are in the trenches just trying to survive. And look, I'm not going to pretend. In some parts of the world, it's still true that women struggle a lot simply for being women. Traditions, and sometimes even laws, still put them at a disadvantage. And in the 21st century, that shouldn't be the case. But most of the influencers painting men as the oppressors and women as the oppressed are from Western countries, mostly the US, and they are generally talking about women's lives there. So a couple of days ago, when I was researching the leading causes of death for women 18 to 44 in the US, you probably saw the video, I did one small thing. On CDC website, I switched the filter from female to male, just to see how different the picture really is. Honestly, I expected some numbers higher for men, some higher for women, but roughly comparable overall. But what I saw genuinely shocked me. And before I show you, I want to be clear about one thing. This is not me complaining that men have it worse. It is me saying we might have it harder than many admit. And very few are talking about it. So here's what I found. Leading causes of death 18 to 44, year 2024, because it's the last available, the only difference is sex. The leading cause of death for women in that group is unintentional injury, about 16,000. For men, 45,000, nearly three times as many. Suicide, for women, around 4,200. For men, 17,000. That's four times higher. Let that sit for a second. Four times as many men in their prime take their own lives. Homicide, the number that whole video was about. For women, about 2,200. For men, 10,500. Almost five times more. And it keeps going. Besides cancer, which is slightly higher for women, every other number on this list is higher for men. And almost always, not just a little higher, dramatically higher. Now, here's the part I keep coming back to. If the numbers for men are this much worse, why does it feel like the opposite? Why does it feel like men are fine and women are the ones under siege? And I think the answer is almost embarrassingly simple. Women talk about their pain. Men don't. When women struggle, they reach out, they post, they organize, they support each other. And that's not a criticism. That's a praise. It's why their problems get seen. Men do the opposite. We go quiet. We handle it alone. We treat asking for help like a failure. So our pain doesn't show up in the conversation. It shows up in that suicide number instead. So you get this picture where it looks like women are the ones suffering and men are living the good life. But the silence isn't proof that men are fine. The silence is the problem. And look, I want to be really careful here because this is exactly where it usually goes wrong. This is not me saying, see, men actually have it worse. So stop complaining. I'm not doing that. That would be the same fight with the team swapped. And that fight gets us nowhere. Here's what I actually see when I look at these two lists side by side. They're almost the same list. Accidents, suicide, heart disease, cancer. Men and women in this age group are mostly dying of the same things. We're not living in two different worlds. We're in the same one fighting a lot of the same battles, often silently, often alone. So why are we acting like enemies? The feminist isn't my opponent. The guy struggling in silence isn't her opponent. We are dealing with overlapping versions of the same human problems. I'm not asking anyone to stop talking about women's struggles. Keep doing it. I'm asking that we make room to talk about men's too. Because right now, that room basically doesn't exist. And men are dying in that silence. A healthy society is not men versus women. It is not who has it worse. It is men and women looking at each other and going, oh, you're hurting too? Let's deal with this together. We need each other to have it better. That's the whole point.
